parts.text: In reality, the total income of a country is not shared equally, so there is income inequality. In 1905 the American economist Max Lorenz invented the Lorenz curve to show income inequality. A Lorenz curve is always on or below the line of perfect equality. The graph shows the Lorenz curve for one country. The point V on this Lorenz curve shows that the poorest 0.7 of the population only earn 0.4 of the total income.

content.tex: In reality, the total income of a country is not shared equally, so there is income inequality. In 1905 the American economist Max Lorenz invented the Lorenz curve to show income inequality. A Lorenz curve is always on or below the line of perfect equality.
The graph shows the Lorenz curve for one country.
The point \(V\) on this Lorenz curve shows that the poorest 0.7 of the population only earn 0.4 of the total income.

parts.text: In 1912 the Italian statistician Corrado Gini invented the Gini coefficient . The Gini coefficient measures how much income inequality there is in a country. The Gini coefficient is two times the shaded area between the line of perfect equality and the Lorenz curve. This means that the greater the shaded area, the greater the income inequality.

parts.text: Mei uses these steps to model the Gini coefficient for the curve in Question 9 . Step 1: Plot point V from Question 9 on the Lorenz curve. Step 2: Approximate the area below the curve with a rectangle and two triangles. Step 3: Calculate the total area of the rectangle and the two triangles. This is T . Step 4: Calculate the shaded area by subtracting T from the area of the large triangle with vertices (0, 0), (1, 1) and (1, 0). Step 5: Multiply the result by 2. Steps 1 and 2 in Mei’s model have been done for you on the graph. Do Steps 3, 4 and 5 to calculate her approximation of the Gini coefficient. ................................................. [6]

content.tex: Mei uses these steps to model the Gini coefficient for the curve in Question 9.

Step 1: Plot point \(V\) from Question 9 on the Lorenz curve. Step 2: Approximate the area below the curve with a rectangle and two triangles. Step 3: Calculate the total area of the rectangle and the two triangles. This is \(T\) . Step 4: Calculate the shaded area by subtracting \(T\) from the area of the large triangle with vertices \((0, 0),\) \((1, 1)\) and \((1, 0).\) Step 5: Multiply the result by 2.
Steps 1 and 2 in Mei’s model have been done for you on the graph.
Do Steps \(3, 4\) and 5 to calculate her approximation of the Gini coefficient.
